title: Syntax and Binding Effects Cluster
text:
Participating projects
This cluster brings together projects

P02 - Grammatcal Gender in Discourse,
P03 - Mismatches in Binding and Coreference,
P05 - The Role of Self in Pronominal Reference,
P06 - The (Non-Deficiency) and (Non-)Redundancy of Clitic Pronouns,
P10 - Deficiency and Redundancy in Expressing Temporal Relations.



Description
The Syntax and Binding Effects cluster has concluded its work after providing a forum for collaboration on syntactic structure and binding-related phenomena. Its activities included reading groups and contributions to the Redefi Days 2025, supporting exchange across the participating subprojects and helping to consolidate shared theoretical interests.

title: Semantics and Discourse Effects Cluster
text:
Participating projects
This cluster brings together projects

P02 - Grammatical Gender in Discourse,
P03 - Mismatches in Binding and Coreference,
P05 - The Role of Self in Pronominal Reference,
P07 - Deficiency and Redundancy in Iberoromance Pronominal Systems,
P08 - Fading Reference - The Pragmaticalization of Pronoun + Verb,
P09 - Animacy Features and the Flexibility of Pronouns,
P10 - Deficiency and Redundancy in Expressing Temporal Relations.



Description
The Semantics and Discourse Effects cluster focuses on the interaction between grammatical structure, meaning, and discourse-related interpretation. Its activities have included reading groups and an internal workshop held in December 2025, providing a forum for discussion across the relevant subprojects.

title: Experimental Methods Cluster
text:
Participating Projects
This cluster brings together projects

P02 - Grammatical Gender in Discourse,
P05 - The Role of Self in Pronominal Coreference,
P07 - Deficiency and Redundancy in Iberoromance Pronominal Systems,
P08 - Fading Reference - The Pragmaticalization of Pronoun + Verb,
P09 - Animacy Features and the Flexibility of Pronouns,

P10 - Deficiency and Redundacy in Expressing Temporal Relations.



Description
The Experimental Methods cluster supports the development and exchange of methodological expertise across the project network. Its activities have included a statistics workshop, a reading group, the establishment of shared infrastructure, and the exchange of practical experience in experimental work. The cluster has also organized an online workshop on conducting online experiments and has maintained close interaction with the Romance cluster.

title: Our team
text:
P01 – Theoretical Task Force





Univ.-Prof. Dr.phil. Edgar Onea








CoordinatorUniversity of Graz


  edgar.onea-gaspar[at]uni-graz.at  Institutional profile


Edgar Onea coordinates the ReDeFi project. He received his doctorate from Heidelberg University in 2005 and subsequently worked at the University of Stuttgart from 2006 to 2010. At the University of Göttingen, he served as Junior Professor from 2010 to 2016 and as W2 Professor from 2016 to 2017. Since September 2017, he has been Professor of German Language and Linguistics at the University of Graz, where he heads the Department of Theoretical and Empirical Linguistics. His current research focuses on text structure and political language. He is also involved in the interdisciplinary FWF- and DFG-funded project “The Erotetic and the Aesthetic: How Linguistic Features of Literary Texts Determine Literary Suspense,” conducted jointly with the University of Göttingen.






Dott.ssa Martina Barili, MA








PhD studentUniversity of Graz


  martina.barili[at]uni-graz.at  Institutional profile


Martina Barili holds a master’s degree in Language and Mind from the University of Siena. Her previous research focused on gradability and vagueness, particularly the semantics of gradable adjectives that express value judgements. Within the ReDeFi project, her current research aims to develop a novel model of grammar that incorporates the properties of redundancy and deficiency.






Nastaran Divani, MA








PhD studentUniversity of Graz

Dr. Sarah Melker








Postdoc researcherUniversity of Graz


  sarah.melker[at]uni-graz.at  Institutional profile


Sarah Melker completed her undergraduate studies in French language and literature at Bryn Mawr College in the United States, followed by a master’s degree at Sciences Po in Paris. In 2018, she returned to higher education to pursue an MSc in Forensic Speech Science at the University of York in the United Kingdom. Her dissertation focused on delocutivisation, a particular type of derivational pathway.







P02 – Grammatical Gender in Discourse and Grammar





Univ.-Prof. Dr.phil. Edgar Onea








Principal InvestigatorUniversity of Graz


  edgar.onea-gaspar[at]uni-graz.at  Institutional profile


Edgar Onea coordinates the ReDeFi project. He received his doctorate from Heidelberg University in 2005 and subsequently worked at the University of Stuttgart from 2006 to 2010. At the University of Göttingen, he served as Junior Professor from 2010 to 2016 and as W2 Professor from 2016 to 2017. Since September 2017, he has been Professor of German Language and Linguistics at the University of Graz, where he heads the Department of Theoretical and Empirical Linguistics. His current research focuses on text structure and political language. He is also involved in the interdisciplinary FWF- and DFG-funded project “The Erotetic and the Aesthetic: How Linguistic Features of Literary Texts Determine Literary Suspense,” conducted jointly with the University of Göttingen.






Simon Dampfhofer, BA BSc MA








PhD studentUniversity of Graz


  simon.dampfhofer[at]uni-graz.at  Institutional profile


Simon Dampfhofer holds an MA in German Linguistics and Philology, for which he wrote a thesis on the semantics of German indefinites, as well as a BSc in Physics. He has also pursued further academic studies in physics and philosophy. His background includes formal semantics, empirical research, and statistical methodology, and he has contributed to the implementation of several experiments at the Institute for German Studies at the University of Graz. He has participated in workshops, conferences, and summer schools, including ÖLT, ICSH, and the DGfS Summer School. His research interests include the syntax and semantics of pronouns, theories of gender, and the philosophy of language.







P03 – Mismatches in Binding and Coreference





Univ.-Prof. Mag., PhD. Susanne Wurmbrand








Principal InvestigatorUniversity of Salzburg


  susanne.wurmbrand[at]plus.ac.at  Institutional profile


Susi Wurmbrand is Professor of Linguistics at Paris Lodron University of Salzburg. She previously held positions at McGill University and the University of Connecticut, as well as a part-time appointment at Harvard University. Her research in theoretical linguistics focuses on syntax and its interfaces. She is a member of the Academia Europaea and holds several editorial positions.






Franziska Keller, BSc., M.A.








PhD studentUniversity of Salzburg


  franziska.keller[at]plus.ac.at  Institutional profile


Franziska Keller is a PhD student at the University of Salzburg and a research assistant in Susanne Wurmbrand’s subproject “Mismatches in Binding and Coreference.” She holds a BSc in General Theoretical Linguistics from the University of Potsdam and an MA in General Linguistics from the University of Vienna. Her research within the subproject examines binding phenomena, particularly the formal and cross-linguistic properties of fake indexicals in relative clauses. Her broader interests include the morphology–syntax interface, root-and-pattern morphology, Arabic languages, resumptive pronouns, and syntactic movement. She has also participated in several conferences and summer schools, including EGG and ÖLT.

P05 – The Role of Self in Pronominal Coreference





Univ.-Prof. PhD Boban Arsenijević








Principal InvestigatorUniversity of Graz


  boban.arsenijevic[at]uni-graz.at  Institutional profile


Boban Arsenijević is Professor of Slavic Linguistics at the University of Graz. He earned a BA in Serbo-Croatian Language and Literature from the University of Niš, an MA in Linguistics from the University of Belgrade, and a Research MA and PhD in Linguistics from Leiden University. His research examines the interfaces of syntax with semantics and phonology, with particular emphasis on Slavic languages. His main interests include verbal aspect and morphology, clausal embedding, and semantic ontology. Within the SFB, he investigates similarities between intensified and reflexive pronouns that may underlie their diachronic and typological connections. His comparative research covers Slavic languages, where intensifiers may receive reflexive interpretations despite being formally distinct; German, where reflexives can combine with intensifiers; and Malayalam and English, where reflexive and intensified pronouns are formally identical.






Aleksandra Milosavljević, Master








PhD studentUniversity of Graz


  aleksandra.milosavljevic[at]uni-graz.at  Institutional profile


Aleksandra Milosavljević is a researcher and PhD student at the University of Graz. She holds MA degrees in Linguistics and Communication Studies from the University of Belgrade. From 2018 to 2024, she worked at the Institute for the Serbian Language of the Serbian Academy of Sciences and Arts. Her research focuses on syntax and semantics, particularly expletive and defective pronouns, clause structure, and verb complements. She has presented her work at conferences including SinFonIJA, FDSL, SLE, and ConSOLE, and has published in Glossa, Balcania et Slavia, and the Proceedings of ConSOLE. Her international academic experience includes the Go Styria exchange programme at the University of Graz and the EGG summer schools.






Joeri Vinke








PhD studentUniversity of Graz


  joeri.vinke[at]uni-graz.at  Institutional profile


Joeri Vinke holds a bachelor’s degree in Linguistics from the University of Groningen and a Research Master’s degree in Linguistics from Utrecht University. His master’s thesis examined Differential Object Marking in heritage languages, with particular attention to Sarnámi Hindustani, an underdescribed East Indo-Aryan heritage language. His broader research interests include relations between arguments, adpositional syntax, the adjunct–argument distinction, and head movement. Within the project, he investigates the interactions among derivational theories of binding, inalienable possession, and intensification, and how these interactions can explain the cross-linguistic patterns examined by the project.







P06 - The (Non-)Deficiency and (Non-)Redundancy of Clitic Pronouns





Assoz. Prof. Dr. Dalina Kallulli








Principal InvestigatorUniversity of Vienna


  dalina.kallulli[at]univie.ac.at  Institutional profile


Dalina Kallulli earned an MA in English from the University of Tirana in 1991, an MPhil in General Linguistics from the University of Trondheim in 1995, and a PhD in Theoretical Linguistics from Durham University in 1999. Following several research fellowships, she joined the University of Vienna as Assistant Professor and was subsequently promoted to Associate Professor. Her research focuses on voice and argument structure, including verbal diminutives, as well as clitic constructions, resumption, relative clauses, and other wh-constructions.






Dr. Adina Camelia Bleotu








Postdoc researcherUniversity of Vienna


  adina.camelia.bleotu[at]univie.ac.at  Institutional profile


Adina Camelia Bleotu is an Assistant Professor at the University of Bucharest. She received her PhD in Linguistics from Ca’ Foscari University of Venice in 2015. Her dissertation on morphological approaches to denominal verbs was subsequently published as a monograph by Brill. She has held fellowships at the University of Massachusetts Amherst and ZAS Berlin, and her research has appeared in journals including Language Acquisition, Glossa, and the Journal of Memory and Language. Her work combines theoretical linguistics, experimental methods, and language acquisition, with particular attention to children’s acquisition of logical operators, recursion, agreement, and strong and weak pronouns. Her current research examines null objects, reflexivity, reflexive clitics, and the Person–Case Constraint.






Dr. Ekaterina Levina








Postdoc researcherUniversity of Vienna


  ekaterina.levina[at]univie.ac.at  Institutional profile


Ekaterina Levina received her PhD in Linguistics from the University of Texas at Austin in 2024. She previously completed an MA in Theoretical Linguistics in 2014 and a BA in German Linguistics and Spanish in 2011 at Humboldt University of Berlin. She also holds a degree in German as a Foreign Language, comparable to a BA, from Leipzig University and a law degree, comparable to a JD, from Saint Petersburg Polytechnic University. Her research connects semantics, syntax, and pragmatics from cross-linguistic and typological perspectives. Her principal interests include definiteness, anaphoric uptake, possessives, event conceptualization, and modality.







P07 — Deficiency and Redundancy in Iberoromance Pronominal Systems





Associate Prof. Mag. Dr. Albert Wall








Principal InvestigatorUniversity of Vienna


  albert.wall[at]univie.ac.at  Institutional profile


Albert Wall received his master’s degree in Romance and East Slavic Philology from the University of Tübingen in 2008 and completed his doctorate in Comparative Romance Linguistics at the University of Zurich in 2015. He joined the University of Vienna in 2020 and was appointed Associate Professor of Romance Linguistics in 2025. His research focuses on argument structure and the syntax and semantics of nominals in Ibero-Romance varieties. He also investigates the syntax–phonology interface and linguistic variation through experimental and other complementary methods. This methodological diversity enables him to examine theoretically significant phenomena that are difficult to observe directly.






Philippa Adolf








PhD studentUniversity of Vienna


  philippa.adolf[at]univie.ac.at  Institutional profile


Philippa Adolf holds a BA in Romance Linguistics and has completed the Bavarian state examination for teaching English and Spanish at secondary level. Her research examines how syntactic, semantic, and discourse-related factors shape direct-object realisation in Spanish, with particular emphasis on differential object marking, clitic doubling, and null objects. She combines corpus and experimental methods and is insterested in modelling linguistic variation quantitatively. Her previous work examines differential object marking in the Spanish of German-speaking learners in comparison with monolingual speakers.






Marco Losavio, MA








PhD studentUniversity of Vienna


  marco.giacomo.losavio[at]univie.ac.at  Institutional profile


Marco holds a master’s degree in Classical Greek Philology from the University of Zurich. His current research examines clitic doubling and null objects in Ibero-Romance varieties, with a particular focus on Brazilian Portuguese and ongoing changes in its pronominal system. His broader interests include historical and comparative linguistics, especially diachronic variation. His master’s thesis investigated the development of perfective periphrases from Ancient Greek to a Modern Greek dialect spoken in Southern Italy.







P08 – Fading Reference – The Pragmaticalization of Pronoun + Verb





Univ.-Prof. Dr. Eva-Maria Remberger








Principal InvestigatorUniversity of Vienna


  eva-maria.remberger[at]univie.ac.at  Institutional profile


Eva Maria Remberger studied Romance Languages and Literatures, German, and English at the University of Cologne, as well as German as a Foreign Language at the University of Bonn. She completed her doctorate at Freie Universität Berlin in 2003. From 2007 to 2008, she was a Feodor Lynen Fellow of the Alexander von Humboldt Foundation at the University of Cambridge and Clare Hall. She served as Junior Professor of Romance Linguistics at the University of Konstanz from 2006 to 2013 and has been Professor of Romance Linguistics at the University of Vienna since 2013. Her research spans grammatical theory, modality, volitionality, evidentiality, discourse-marker development, and the morphology and formal pragmatics of Romance languages from synchronic and diachronic perspectives. She also investigates language contact and connections among migrant languages, Romance languages, and Latin in language teaching and subject didactics.






Andrea Miglietta, MA








PhD studentUniversity of Vienna


  andrea.miglietta[at]univie.ac.at  Institutional profile


Andrea Miglietta holds a BA in Humanities and an MA in Linguistics from the University of Bologna. His research focuses on interactions between pronouns and verbs in Italian. In his master’s thesis, he investigated the semantic boundaries of Italian restructuring verbs, using clitic climbing as a diagnostic. His subsequent work examines pronouns in Italian deverbal discourse markers and uses corpus data to develop morphosyntactic models of discourse-oriented elements. His broader research interests include epistemic modality, grammaticalization, and parenthetical verbs.






Ignasi Planas Villalba, BA








Student assistantUniversity of Vienna


  ignasi.planas.villalba[at]univie.ac.at  Institutional profile


Ignasi holds a master’s degree in General Linguistics from the University of Vienna, for which he wrote a thesis on the role of kinship in nominal morphosyntax under the supervision of Dalina Kallulli. His research examines the pragmaticalization of pronoun–verb sequences in Catalan, such as (jo) crec (“I believe”), and their development into discourse markers expressing epistemicity and related meanings. His broader interests include comparative morphosyntax, particularly in Romance languages. He also organizes the VII Jornades de Lingüística Catalana a Viena.







P09 – Animacy Features and the Flexibility of Pronouns





Assoz. Prof. Mag. Dr. Steffen Heidinger








Principal InvestigatorUniversity of Graz


  steffen.heidinger[at]uni-graz.at  Institutional profile


Steffen Heidinger is Associate Professor of Romance Linguistics at the University of Graz. He completed his doctorate in 2008 within a Franco-German graduate programme involving the universities of Stuttgart and Paris 8. His dissertation examined the diachronic development of French anticausatives. In 2017, he completed his habilitation in Romance Linguistics at the University of Graz with a thesis on the information-structural properties of Spanish depictives. His current research focuses on the animacy features of French and Spanish pronouns. Within the subproject “Animacy Features and the Flexibility of Pronouns,” he investigates whether particular pronoun types are specified for animacy and how redundancy and deficiency license uses that diverge from these specifications, such as strong pronouns referring to inanimate entities.






Dr. Yanis da Cunha, Master








Postdoc researcherUniversity of Graz


  yanis.da-cunha[at]uni-graz.at  Institutional profile


Yanis da Cunha is a researcher in Romance Linguistics at the University of Graz. His doctoral research at Université Paris Cité examines gender effects on grammatical-function assignment, including biases that favour male subjects and female objects. More broadly, he investigates the factors underlying syntactic alternations, particularly variation in voice and word order across English, French, Modern Greek, and Spanish. Within the subproject “Animacy Features and the Flexibility of Pronouns,” he studies the role of gender in French and Spanish pronominal systems. His research explores how grammatical gender affects the animacy restrictions associated with certain pronouns, including French strong pronouns, and how pronouns accommodate mismatches between grammatical and semantic gender, such as reference to gender-underspecified nouns.

Melanie Loitzl, BA BA BEd MA








PhD studentUniversity of Vienna


  melanie.loitzl[at]univie.ac.at  Institutional profile


Before beginning her doctoral studies in Vienna, Melanie Loitzl completed bachelor’s degrees in German Studies, English and American Studies, and Teacher Education in German and English at the University of Graz. She subsequently earned a master’s degree in German Studies there, with a thesis on the use and interpretation of directional adverbs in Bavarian, and is currently completing a master’s degree in Teacher Education. Her doctoral research examines the formal properties of temporal adverbs and their interaction with tense, with particular attention to indexical expressions such as yesterday and today and complex expressions such as Monday evening and early this morning. She combines formal analysis in semantics and syntax with empirical methods, building on experience gained as a student assistant at the Department of German Studies in Graz.

Justina Schindler holds a bachelor’s degree in Linguistics from Leipzig University and a master’s degree in General Linguistics from the University of Vienna. She also spent a year studying logic at the University of Amsterdam. Her primary research interest is formal semantics, with a particular focus on the interaction between tense and temporal quantification.

title: Welcome to the SFB Language between Redundancy and Deficiency
text:
universities projects members




Welcome to the SFB Language between Redundancy and Deficiency

Language is one of our most fundamental cognitive capacities. This Special Research Area (SFB) Network is developing a new approach to modeling the linguistic system. The starting point is the hypothesis that the cognitive core of language ability is based on logical-symbolic calculations, but is embedded in a cognitive system of stochastic nature. As an interface between the symbolic and stochastic components, grammar uses the central optimization factors of redundancy and deficiency, which can underlie linguistic operations and make it possible to process both under- and over-specified inputs.
The Network brings together the particularly strong linguistic research at the Universities of Graz, Vienna, and Salzburg and deals with uniformly defined, comprehensive empirical areas of grammar (pronouns and ellipsis). The sub-projects illuminate, classify and model these theoretically and empirically from the perspective of the concepts of redundancy and deficiency. Expected findings not only promise a deeper understanding of the basic mechanisms of the grammatical system, but also open up new perspectives for central questions in cognitive science regarding the role of language in cognition.
This Research Network is financed by the Austrian Science Fund for Special Research Areas (SFB Grant F1003).

title: Corpus and Annotation Cluster
text:
Participating projects
This cluster brings together projects

P02 - Grammatical Gender in Discourse,
P07 - Deficinecy and Redundancy in Iberoromance Pronominal Systems,
P08 - Fading Reference - The Pragmaticalization of Pronoun + Verb.



Description
The Corpus and Annotation cluster has produced a repository of corpora for Romance languages, covering Spanish and Italian and, to a more limited extent, Portuguese and Catalan. It functions as a network used for consultation between projects working with both custom and existing corpora. The repository provides descriptions of the individual corpora together with access links where available, creating a shared resource for corpus-based research across the project network.

title: Romance Data Cluster
text:
Participating projects
This cluster brings together projects

P06 - The (Non-)Deficiency and (Non-)Redundancy of Clitic Pronouns,
P07 - Deficiency and Redundancy in Iberoromance Pronominal Systems,
P08 - Fading Reference - The Pragmaticalization of Pronoun + Verb,
P09 - Animacy Features and the Flexibility of Pronouns.



Description
The Romance Data cluster focuses on collaborative empirical work across Romance languages and varieties. A central activity has been a data-sharing initiative designed to facilitate access to relevant empirical materials across subprojects, alongside coordinated experimental work. One concrete outcome of this collaboration is a cross-Romance experiment on null objects across eight Romance varieties, involving subprojects P01, P06, P07, and P09 and extending cooperation beyond the immediate cluster.

Description
The Zero Elements cluster brings together research on structures in which linguistic material is absent, omitted, or not overtly realized. Its activities have been closely linked to the Romance cluster, reflecting substantial overlap in the empirical domains investigated by the participating projects, such as null or zero pronominal elements and ellipsis phenomena.

title: Clitic Pronouns Cluster
text:
Participating projects
This cluster brings together projects

P06 - The (Non-)Deficiency and (Non-)Redundancy of Clitic Pronouns,
P07 - Deficiency and Redundancy in Iberoromance Pronominal Systems,
P08 - Fading Referene - The Pragmaticalization of Pronoun + Verb,
P09 - Animacy Feattures and the Flexibility of Pronouns.



Description
The Clitic Pronouns cluster brings together work on clitic systems and related grammatical phenomena across the participating subprojects. Its activities are focused on reading groups and have been closely connected to the Romance cluster, allowing the projects involved to coordinate analyses and empirical work where clitic pronouns intersect with broader questions concerning Romance grammar.
